## A Model Call in the Stochastic Computer {#sec-vol3-processor-role}

A classical processor operates as a deterministic execution unit governed by an instruction set architecture (ISA): advancing an instruction pointer, decoding explicit opcodes, executing within hardware privilege levels (such as user and kernel rings), and mutating registers and memory. Illegal opcodes, unmapped virtual memory accesses, or arithmetic faults trigger synchronous hardware exceptions, halting execution or trapping to kernel handlers before state corruption propagates unchecked. In stark contrast, a foundation model in an agentic architecture functions as an unprivileged, non-deterministic execution unit: a stochastic processor core. Within the volume's four-dimensional workload taxonomy—spanning Horizon ($H$), State Complexity ($S$), Authority ($A$), and Invariant Closure ($C$)—a single model invocation represents the minimal atomic execution step of the Stochastic Computer, evaluated at the baseline coordinate ($H=1, S=\text{staged}, A=0, C=\text{external}$). This coordinate defines an atomic, single-step invocation horizon ($H=1$) operating over static context staged in memory escrow ($S=\text{staged}$), possessing zero ambient authority to mutate external state ($A=0$), and requiring external runtime verification to certify invariant closure ($C=\text{external}$). When energized by staged input tokens, the neural core advances no program counter and modifies no host registers. Instead, it evaluates a learned conditional probability distribution over a discrete vocabulary under zero ambient authority.[^fn-zero-ambient-authority] Possessing no privilege rings, interrupt lines, or direct visibility into host state, its emissions are not executable commands, but passive statistical hypotheses awaiting external interpretation.

[^fn-zero-ambient-authority]: **Zero Ambient Authority** (Systems Architecture / Clarification): An execution model formalized in modern object-capability literature [@miller2003; @miller2006robust], contrasting with ambient systems where execution contexts implicitly inherit ambient privileges. In the Stochastic Computer, the neural core holds no implicit permissions to mutate host state, adhering to @saltzer1975's principle of least privilege. \index{Zero Ambient Authority}\index{Security!Zero Ambient Authority}\index{Least Privilege}

In traditional computer architectures, the ISA guarantees that anomalous machine states trigger explicit architectural exceptions (such as page faults or illegal instruction traps).[^fn-fail-stop] The stochastic processor core exhibits no such exception mechanism at the semantic level. Because forward computation consists of continuous matrix transformations across learned parameter tensors $\Theta$, the core does not trap or halt when presented with an underspecified interface, missing parameters, or contradictory context. Instead, within valid numerical bounds, it exhibits fail-plausible behavior: emitting fluent symbols that assert false facts, invent nonexistent paths, or generate invalid syntax while maintaining high statistical likelihood. Emitting text resembling a shell script or database mutation modifies zero bytes of host storage; the output remains a candidate proposal held in memory escrow. The host system must treat every output not as an action taken, but as an unverified hypothesis whose operational validity must be established entirely outside the model.

[^fn-fail-stop]: **Fail-Stop Model** (Historical / Context): A dependability model introduced by @schlichting1983failstop where a processor operates according to specification or halts upon internal failure. Neural execution cores violate this model at the semantic level by continuing to generate syntactically well-formed sequences when operational validity has collapsed. \index{Fail-Stop Model}\index{Historical!Fail-Stop Model}\index{Fault Tolerance!Fail-Stop Model}

To govern this stochastic core without sacrificing systems integrity, the architecture partitions execution across a three-tier operational boundary (@fig-stochastic-processor-core). At the highest level sits the Host Agent Runtime, operating in user-space CPU memory as the software counterpart of an operating system supervisor. The runtime owns task orchestration, compiles structural schemas into grammar automata, stages prompt context into memory escrow, enforces resource limits, and mediates actuation. Beneath it lies the Inference Service Daemon, an accelerator driver managing request queues, tokenizing raw byte streams into discrete token IDs, scheduling tensor batches, maintaining Key-Value (KV) cache buffers in device memory, and applying decode-time logit masks during sampling. At the lowest level operates the Neural Core: static parameter tensors $\Theta$ executing tensor contractions on accelerator compute units, evaluating matrix multiplications: general matrix multiply (GEMM) during prompt prefill and general matrix-vector multiply (GEMV) during autoregressive decode. Crucially, the neural core maps hidden activations to raw unnormalized logit vectors $\mathbf{z} \in \mathbb{R}^{|\mathcal{V}|}$; only after the inference service applies softmax normalization does the resulting distribution span the probability simplex $\Delta^{|\mathcal{V}|-1}$, from which candidate token IDs are sampled and streamed back across the host interconnect bus.

::: {#fig-stochastic-processor-core fig-cap="**Three-Tier Invocation Lifecycle**: Boundary separation between host runtime, inference service daemon, and neural execution core across staging, generation, and verification phases." fig-alt="The three-tier invocation lifecycle showing host runtime, inference service, and neural core."}
![](images/svg/invocation_lifecycle.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Maintaining this three-tier boundary requires that each layer preserve its separation of concerns. An architectural vulnerability arises whenever systems blur these responsibilities, such as expecting the neural core to enforce its own safety perimeters or requiring the host CPU to parse vocabulary logit distributions. The host runtime compiles a structural grammar into an automaton, but transmitting unnormalized logit vectors—exceeding one hundred thousand floating-point values per decode step—across interconnect buses would saturate bandwidth and collapse decoding throughput. Consequently, the host runtime delegates the compiled automaton to the inference service daemon, which executes logit masking directly within device memory before sampling each token. Conversely, the inference service treats candidate token streams as passive payload bytes; it neither evaluates the semantic validity of emitted code nor grants execution privileges. The boundary between proposing a candidate symbol sequence and authorizing an environmental mutation remains absolute.[^fn-reference-monitor]

[^fn-reference-monitor]: **Reference Monitor** (Historical / Context): An access control mechanism formulated by Anderson [@anderson1972computer] and codified under @saltzer1975's principle of complete mediation, requiring that every access to host resources be validated by an authoritative, tamper-proof monitor. In the Stochastic Computer, the host agent runtime serves as this reference monitor, standing between unprivileged candidate token buffers and physical actuation. \index{Reference Monitor}\index{Security!Reference Monitor}\index{Complete Mediation}

Because the stochastic processor core cannot certify invariant closure internally ($C=\text{external}$), every invocation requires an explicit caller contract governed by resource bounds and deterministic post-conditions. The host runtime wraps each call in explicit ceilings: an emission token limit $K_{\max}$ bounding decoding steps, and an end-to-end deadline $T_{\max}$ bounding latency. When generation terminates, the runtime receives a normalized status envelope categorizing termination into one of seven mutually exclusive primary outcomes: normal completion (`COMPLETED`), resource exhaustion (`TRUNCATED`), policy suppression (`REFUSED`), communication failure (`TRANSPORT_FAILURE`), admission rejection (`REJECTED`), client abort (`CANCELLED`), or unrecoverable execution fault (`FAULTED`), paired with machine-parseable reason codes. Only when an invocation terminates as `COMPLETED` does the runtime extract the candidate proposal from escrow and submit it to external deterministic validation tools—such as static linters, Abstract Syntax Tree parsers, type checkers, and test suites. If an output terminates abnormally or violates an external assertion, the runtime intercepts the fault, preventing corrupted state from propagating into host state.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/option1_hsac_compact.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="H-S-A-C workload diamond highlighting the single-step invocation horizon (H=1) and zero ambient authority (A=0), operating with staged context complexity (S=staged) and external invariant closure (C=external)."}

*The stochastic processor operates at the single-step baseline ($H=1, A=0$).*
:::

Treating the foundation model as a stochastic processor core establishes the boundary between statistical token emission and authoritative system execution. Yet this formulation exposes an immediate foundational question at the hardware-software boundary. A classical processor operates upon binary words, integer memory addresses, and structured opcodes defined by an instruction set architecture. The neural core, however, operates upon continuous activation vectors mapped to discrete integer indices across a fixed vocabulary. Before data can cross into this processor core, how must it be formatted and encoded?
